On the retained earnings comments

Think about if retained earnings were not invested in the business.  Prior to earning the retained earnings the company would have a factory and make stuff.  In order for it to grow it would have to get better at making stuff with the same factory and that's "true" growth.  

Said another way.  If a company decided to buy another company with debt or cash on the balance sheet And let's say the company purchased had 50% of the earnings of the first company

Clearly absolute earnings growth would be 50% (less when adjusted for debt interest) but still huge and the old company earnings would fall out of the sample of earnings growth EPS would also grow of the survivor

Retained earnings reinvested in factories is identical to that corporate acquisition.  In other words you can buy earnings growth.

Positioning tells you how crowded a trade is. The source of marginal demand could tell you how durable it may be.

Business activity can create recurring buying pressure that remains after sentiment cools. A durable supply sink can also support price by reducing the amount available to trade.

Momentum-driven positions behave differently. Rising prices attract more capital through a thin market, but that demand weakens when the rally stalls.

This is why co-movement says little about durability. Assets can sell off together without being supported in the same way.

The important question is where the support is after momentum turns.

Our new report "The Crowded Book" is live!

Why do crowded trades that fall together recover so differently?

Every rally needs continued demand. In a funded trade, that demand comes from cash flow or a supply sink that persists independently of price. Borrowed crowding relies on momentum and a thin float so demand weakens when prices stop rising.

The difference became clear in June. A sharp decline in Zcash triggered by a year-old exploit ignited a high-beta selloff across a weak market, pulling Hyperliquid and Venice down as well.

Hyperliquid’s recovery was supported by daily buybacks funded with 97% of trading fees and by a contributor team that kept restaking its unlocks instead of selling into them.

Zcash had no equivalent link to cash flow or usage. Its bid was based on scarcity, with the share of supply held in its shielded pool rising from roughly 8% to 30% over two years, backed by treasury vehicles accumulating alongside it. That steadily reduced the amount available to trade.

Venice had a growing product that most users could access without the token. Consumer growth did not translate directly into token demand. Relatively little supply was available to trade which made the price more sensitive to market flows in either direction.

That is why crowded trades that fall together recover apart. The recovery tests what was paying for the bid.
